## Understanding the Basics of Moving to Italy From US

Its strategic position in Europe opens doors to the continent’s markets, making it appealing for entrepreneurs and remote workers alike. Quality of life factors such as excellent healthcare, a strong emphasis on community, and access to diverse climates—from coastal to alpine regions—add to Italy’s appeal. These qualities make Italy a compelling choice for Americans searching for a life enriched by culture and opportunity.

### Key Challenges Americans Face When Moving to Italy

Moving to Italy from US isn’t without its hurdles. One primary challenge is navigating Italy’s complex visa and residency permit system. Depending on your reason for moving—work, study, family reunification, or retirement—the type of visa you need and its processing times can vary significantly. Language presents another barrier when moving to Italy from US. While English is common in business and tourist areas, day-to-day life often requires some level of Italian proficiency. Logistics also pose difficulties. Shipping household items overseas involves stringent customs regulations and duty taxes that can complicate timing and cost projections. ## Immigration and Legal Considerations for Americans Moving to Italy

### Understanding Visa Options and Residency Permits

When moving to Italy from US, understanding the visa landscape is critical to ensuring a smooth and legal relocation. Italy offers several visa categories depending on the purpose of your stay. For Americans planning to work, the work visa is the most common, requiring a job offer and approval from Italian authorities. Students moving for educational opportunities can apply for a student visa, which also allows limited part-time work.

Family reunification visas enable close relatives of Italian residents or citizens to join them, while the elective residence visa is designed for retirees or those financially independent who seek to live in Italy without working locally. Each visa type has distinct requirements, documentation needs, and application timelines. Selecting the correct visa early prevents complications and legal issues after arrival.

### How to Immigrate to Italy From US Successfully

Successfully immigrating to Italy involves a step-by-step process when moving to Italy from US. First, determine which visa matches your situation, then gather all necessary documents—passport, proof of income, health insurance, and background checks are often required. It’s essential to submit the visa application well ahead of your intended move, as processing times can range from a few weeks to several months.

Once approved, entering Italy with the proper visa is just the beginning for those moving to Italy from US. You must apply for a residency permit (permesso di soggiorno) within eight days of arrival. This permit confirms your legal residence status and is mandatory for longer stays. Application involves a visit to the local police headquarters (Questura) and submitting biometric data.

Advice from experienced international movers like EarthRelo can be invaluable during this phase. Their knowledgeable agents often connect clients with expert legal resources to help navigate Italy’s immigration system, minimizing delays and errors.

### Navigating Italian Bureaucracy After Arrival

**Italian bureaucracy is famously intricate for individuals moving to Italy from US**. After securing your residency permit, registering with local authorities at your town hall (Comune) is mandatory. This process includes enrolling in the Anagrafe, Italy’s registry of residents, which triggers access to essential services.

Obtaining a codice fiscale is another vital step after moving to Italy from US. This tax identification number is required for nearly all administrative duties, including signing leases, opening bank accounts, and accessing healthcare. Without a codice fiscale, many routine activities become difficult or impossible.

Healthcare enrollment follows registration. Italy’s public healthcare system (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale) provides residents access to comprehensive medical care. Registering ensures you receive a health card (tessera sanitaria) and access to doctors and hospitals. EarthRelo’s guidance through these formalities helps Americans transitioning from the US understand what documents and appointments are needed.

### Rights and Responsibilities as an American Expat in Italy

Living legally in Italy means embracing certain rights and responsibilities when moving to Italy from US. As an American expat, you must adhere to local laws, including tax regulations. Italy and the US have tax treaties to prevent double taxation, but it’s essential to file taxes correctly in both countries, often with professional advice.

Maintaining US citizenship while residing in Italy is straightforward when moving to Italy from US, but keeping passports up to date and complying with US regulations such as the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) is necessary. Additionally, understanding voting rights and consular support options can ease your life abroad.

Respecting Italian customs, laws, and community standards is equally important. EarthRelo offers support beyond logistics by connecting clients with cultural resources and legal advisors, helping American expats settle confidently into their new lives.

Grasping these immigration and legal considerations forms the backbone of a successful transition when moving to Italy from US. With the right knowledge and reliable support, such as the tailored services provided by EarthRelo, the complexities of relocating internationally become manageable, allowing you to focus on enjoying your new Italian chapter.

Whether you choose to rent or buy, understanding the local real estate landscape is essential for Americans new to the market. Popular Italian cities offer diverse neighborhoods, each with unique characteristics. For example, Rome’s Trastevere district is known for its vibrant social scene and historic charm, while Milan’s Porta Nuova area appeals to professionals with its modern amenities.

Outside major cities, regions like Tuscany or Liguria provide tranquil alternatives but may involve less English-speaking support and fewer available rentals. While some Italians speak English, especially in urban centers, grasping Italian phrases and conversational skills dramatically eases daily interactions. Language schools, apps, and community classes are excellent resources that EarthRelo encourages clients to explore early on.

Cultural customs are equally important for those moving to Italy from US. Italians place great value on hospitality, punctuality is more relaxed, and meal times revolve around social connection, often stretching for hours. Understanding these social rhythms fosters smoother local relationships. Simple habits, like greeting neighbors and respecting quiet hours, help build goodwill.

Moreover, practical differences — such as how shops close on Sundays or the importance of recycling rules — can take some getting used to. Building a support network is vital when moving to Italy from US. Connecting with fellow Americans and international expats eases feelings of isolation and offers valuable insights. Italy hosts active expat communities across major cities, organizing social events, cultural outings, and even business meetups.

Joining local clubs, language exchange groups, or volunteering projects accelerates integration for individuals moving to Italy from US while preserving cultural identity. Many Americans find that attending Italian festivals and cooking classes not only enriches their experience but also deepens community ties.

EarthRelo recognizes the importance of this social support and frequently shares contacts to expat groups and community hubs with clients, fostering connections that enhance the relocation experience beyond logistics.

Taxation is complex, especially for Americans moving to Italy from US who must file US taxes while paying local obligations. Consulting a tax professional familiar with US-Italy treaties ensures compliance and helps avoid double taxation.

By understanding Italian banking norms and financial systems early on, Americans moving to Italy as an American expat can avoid common pitfalls and manage their money confidently. ## What to Know Before Importing a Non-EU Vehicle

Shipping a vehicle as part of an international relocation to Italy is possible, but it is one of the most regulated and often misunderstood aspects of moving to Italy from the USA. Nilson Van & Storage helps clients understand these realities upfront so they can make informed, cost-effective decisions as part of their overall relocation strategy.

### **Key considerations when shipping a vehicle to Italy include:**

#### EU Emissions and Technical Compliance

Non-EU vehicles must meet European Union emissions and safety standards. Many U.S. vehicles do not comply without modifications, which can be costly and time-consuming once the vehicle arrives in Italy.

#### Import Taxes and VAT Exposure

Depending on residency status, length of stay, and vehicle ownership history, import duties or VAT may apply. These charges can significantly impact the total cost of shipping a vehicle to Italy.

#### Registration and Approval Complexity

Registering a non-EU vehicle in Italy often involves inspections, technical certifications, and extensive paperwork. The process can vary by region and may take several months to complete.

#### Vehicle Age and Condition Restrictions

Older vehicles or specialty models may face additional scrutiny or may not be eligible for registration at all under Italian regulations.

#### Temporary vs. Permanent Import Rules

Some relocations allow for temporary vehicle imports under specific conditions, while permanent imports involve stricter compliance. Understanding which category applies is essential before shipping.

#### Port Handling and Delivery Coordination

Vehicles shipped to Italy must clear customs and be released at designated ports. Storage charges can accrue quickly if documentation or approvals are delayed.

Because of these factors, vehicle shipping is not always the best option for every relocation. In many cases, purchasing or leasing a vehicle locally in Italy may be more practical and economical than importing a U.S. vehicle.

### **Essential steps to complete before shipping to Italy include:**

#### Secure Your Codice Fiscale

The Codice Fiscale is Italy’s tax identification number and is required for many administrative processes, including customs clearance. Without it, shipments may be delayed at port. Applying for this early is one of the most important steps when moving to Italy from the USA.

#### Apply for Permesso di Soggiorno

A Permesso di Soggiorno, or proof that you have applied for one, is often required for customs clearance in Italy. Even if the permit is still being processed, documentation showing your legal residency status can be critical for releasing household goods.

#### Finalize Housing or Temporary Accommodation

Customs and delivery coordination often require proof of address in Italy. Whether you have permanent housing or temporary accommodations arranged, having documentation in place helps prevent delivery delays and storage charges.

#### Prepare a Detailed Inventory

Italian customs requires a clear, itemized inventory of all household goods being shipped. Accurate descriptions help avoid inspections and speed up customs clearance. Inventories should reflect used household goods intended for personal use.

#### Review Restricted and Prohibited Items

Certain items cannot be shipped to Italy or may be subject to restrictions. Reviewing these items before packing helps avoid customs complications and last-minute shipment changes.

#### Align Arrival and Delivery Dates

Coordinating your arrival in Italy with your shipment timeline is essential. Many deliveries require the owner or an authorized representative to be present. Proper alignment reduces storage needs and ensures smoother final delivery.

### Full Container Load (FCL) Shipping

Full Container Load (FCL) shipping is the most comprehensive and secure option for clients relocating an entire household when moving to Italy from the USA. With FCL, your belongings are loaded into a dedicated ocean container that is used exclusively for your shipment from origin to destination. This method offers greater control, faster transit, and reduced risk—making it the preferred choice for families, corporate professionals, and long-term relocations.

For clients shipping a significant volume of furniture, personal effects, and household goods, FCL shipping provides predictability and efficiency throughout the international moving process. Nilson Van and Storage carefully evaluates shipment size, destination access, and delivery requirements to determine whether FCL is the best solution for your move to Italy.

#### Exclusive Use of the Container

Your household goods occupy the entire container, meaning there is no consolidation with other shipments. This minimizes handling, reduces exposure to delays caused by other cargo, and provides greater accountability from origin to delivery in Italy.

#### Faster and More Predictable Transit Times

Because FCL shipments are not dependent on consolidation schedules, they typically move through ports more quickly than shared shipments. This can result in shorter overall transit times when shipping household goods to Italy.

#### Reduced Handling and Lower Risk of Damage

With fewer transfer points and no mixing with other shipments, FCL significantly reduces the number of times your belongings are handled. This added control enhances shipment security and lowers the risk of loss or damage during international transit.

#### Better Option for Tight Delivery Windows

Clients relocating for work, military assignments, or fixed housing availability often benefit from the scheduling reliability that FCL shipping provides. This is especially important when coordinating customs clearance Italy procedures and final delivery.

#### Ideal for Shuttle Services in Italy

When delivery access requires shuttle services due to narrow streets or restricted zones, FCL shipments allow for more efficient trans-shipping coordination, as all goods arrive together in a single container.

#### Scalable for Larger Homes and Long-Term Moves

FCL is well suited for three-bedroom homes, villas, and long-term relocations where most household contents are being moved overseas.

Nilson Van and Storage manages the entire FCL process—from container planning and export packing in the United States to customs clearance and final delivery in Italy. This door-to-door approach ensures that your relocation remains controlled, transparent, and professionally coordinated at every stage.

### Less than Container Load (LCL) / Groupage

Less than Container Load (LCL) shipping, also known as groupage, is an efficient solution for clients who are moving to Italy from the USA with a smaller volume of household goods. Instead of reserving an entire container, your shipment is consolidated with other compatible shipments bound for Italy, allowing you to pay only for the space you use.

LCL shipping is especially popular among retirees, apartment relocations, and clients who are downsizing before an international move. When managed properly by experienced international moving to Italy from USA, groupage shipments provide a reliable balance between cost efficiency and professional handling.

#### Lower Cost for Smaller Shipments

LCL allows you to ship a portion of your household goods without the expense of a full container. This makes it an attractive option for clients seeking to control moving costs to Italy while still receiving professional international relocation services.

#### Pay Only for the Space You Use

With groupage shipping, pricing is based on volume rather than container size. This flexibility benefits clients shipping select furniture, personal effects, or essentials when moving to Italy from the USA.

#### Ideal for Apartments and Downsized Moves

LCL is well suited for apartment relocations, temporary overseas assignments, and situations where only part of a household is being shipped internationally.

#### Professional Consolidation and Handling

Shipments are professionally consolidated at secure facilities and loaded according to international standards. Nilson Van and Storage ensures proper packing, labeling, and segregation to maintain shipment integrity throughout transit.

#### Reliable Door-to-Door Coordination

Even though shipments are shared, LCL moves still follow a structured door-to-door process, including export packing, international transit, customs clearance Italy coordination, and final delivery.

#### Compatible with Shuttle Services in Italy

Like FCL shipments, LCL deliveries may require shuttle services due to narrow streets or restricted access. Groupage shipments are planned accordingly to ensure smooth final delivery in historic city centers and small towns.

It is important to note that LCL shipments may have slightly longer transit times due to consolidation and deconsolidation processes at origin and destination ports. However, with proper planning and realistic expectations, LCL remains a dependable and economical option for shipping household goods to Italy.

Nilson Van and Storage manages every step of the LCL process with transparency and expertise, ensuring your move to Italy remains organized, efficient, and professionally supported from start to finish.

### Air Freight (Limited Use)

Air freight shipping to Italy is the fastest international transportation option, but it is also the most selective in terms of use. For clients moving to Italy from the USA, air freight is rarely used for full household relocations. Instead, it is best suited for essential, time-sensitive items that are needed immediately upon arrival.

Because air freight costs are calculated by weight and volume at a premium rate, careful planning is essential to determine whether this option makes logistical and financial sense for your move to Italy.

### **Situations where air freight makes sense when moving to Italy from the USA:**

#### Immediate Living Essentials

Air freight is ideal for clothing, personal items, important documents, work equipment, or children’s necessities that you need as soon as you arrive in Italy.

#### **Temporary Housing Transitions**

Clients moving into short-term accommodations often use air freight to bridge the gap while their sea shipment is in transit, especially when permanent housing is not yet available.

#### Corporate or Time-Sensitive Assignments

Professionals relocating on fixed start dates may require immediate access to specific items for work or daily life, making air freight a practical short-term solution.

#### Supplement to Sea Freight

Air freight is commonly used alongside FCL or LCL shipments, allowing essential items to arrive quickly while the majority of household goods move by sea.

### Situations where air freight may not be practical:

#### Full Household Moves

Air freight is not cost-effective for furniture, appliances, or large volumes of household goods. For most clients, sea freight remains the preferred option for shipping household goods to Italy.

#### Heavy or Bulky Items

Large furniture pieces, mattresses, and appliances incur very high air freight charges and are better suited for FCL or LCL shipping methods.

#### Budget-Conscious Relocations

Clients focused on controlling overall moving costs to Italy typically limit air freight to a small, carefully selected portion of their belongings.

### Key considerations for air freight shipments to Italy:

#### Strict Packing and Weight Limits

Air shipments must meet airline packaging standards, which differ from ocean freight requirements. Export-grade packing remains essential to protect items during transit.

#### Customs Clearance Still Applies

Even though air freight moves faster, shipments must still undergo customs clearance Italy procedures. Required documentation such as passport details, Codice Fiscale, and residence status must be in place.

#### Faster Transit, Higher Cost

Transit times may range from a few days to two weeks, but this speed comes at a significantly higher cost compared to sea freight.

## Simplifying the Most Stressful Part of Moving to Italy

For most clients, customs clearance in Italy is the single biggest concern—and with good reason. Italian customs, known as _La Dogana_, is thorough, documentation-driven, and unforgiving of errors. Small mistakes can result in port delays, inspections, or costly demurrage charges.

Nilson Van & Storage helps eliminate uncertainty by guiding you through the process well before your shipment leaves the United States.

The Franchigia (Duty-Free Import of Household Goods)

Key Documents for Customs Clearance Italy

The Franchigia (Duty-Free Import of Household Goods)

Italy allows duty-free import of used household goods under the _Franchigia_ provision, provided specific conditions are met. This typically applies when:

- You are relocating your primary residence
- Goods have been owned and used prior to shipment
- Documentation is complete and accurate

Key Documents for Customs Clearance Italy

While requirements can vary slightly by situation, most relocations require:

- Valid passport
- Codice Fiscale (Italian tax identification number)
- Permesso di Soggiorno (residence permit or proof of application)
- Detailed inventory of household goods
- Proof of residence in Italy (lease or property deed)

Without documents such as the Codice Fiscale, shipments may not be released. Our team ensures documentation is reviewed in advance and coordinated with Italian agents to minimize risk.

How do international moves work?

When you move overseas, your stuff can be delivered by boat or by plane, though ocean freight is much [cheaper than air freight](https://www.move.org/international-moving-cost/). You can also opt to have your stuff delivered to your home in your new country or to the nearest port of entry where you can pick it up yourself. Read [our guide to international moving](https://www.move.org/what-to-know-moving-internationally/) to learn more about this process.

### You probably can’t take everything to Italy

No matter what you do, you should plan to spend several thousand dollars on an international move. You can lower your price by [downsizing before leaving](https://www.move.org/how-to-donate-your-used-items/), though. And there are a few things you either can’t or shouldn’t take with you anyway.

Every country has a list of items you’re prohibited from importing, and Italy is no exception. Italy restricts how much meat, dairy, alcohol, and cigarettes you can bring through customs, and that’s just a short list. Check the European Union’s resource on [prohibited items](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/travel/carry/index_en.htm) or talk to your moving company to learn more.

You can also save a small fortune by selling or [donating](https://www.move.org/charity-pick-up/) bulky furniture, clothes you haven’t worn in years, and other items you don’t need or can easily replace once you’re in Italy.

#### Bringing your electronics to Italy

Electronics you’ve purchased in the US, especially ones with motors, are among the first things you should get rid of before your move.

Even if you get an adapter to make your American electronics work with Italian outlets, the difference in power output can fry your tech and appliances unless you invest in a voltage converter.

Overall, it might be better to just replace your electronics with Italian counterparts once you’ve moved. That way, you don’t have to pay your movers to ship gadgets and machines that will give you grief in your new home.

#### Taking your pets to Italy

The good news: you can bring pets to Italy with you. The bad news: it’s a convoluted process and there are many restrictions. In order to bring a cat or dog to Italy, you have to ensure it has the following:

- A vet certificate
- A rabies vaccine
- A tattoo or microchip
- A carrier labeled with your name, Italian address, and phone number

Also, your pet must be at least three months old when you bring it, and—once in Italy—you’ll need to get your pet an EU Pet Passport from an Italian vet. [\[1\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources) And we agree, it really should be called a “pawsport.”

There are other restrictions for animals like birds, fish, reptiles, and rodents, and you can only bring up to five pets into Italy with you. To learn more, check out the US embassy’s resource on [taking animals to Italy](https://it.usembassy.gov/embassy-consulates/rome/sections-offices/foreign-agricultural-service/pet-travel-faqs-italy-u-s/).

#### Taking your vehicle to Italy

You can [ship a car internationally](https://www.move.org/how-do-i-ship-my-car-internationally/), but it can cost more than $5,000 to do so. And that’s just the shipping cost. Italy also charges import taxes, duties, and registration fees for imported cars. Because of these exorbitant costs, you should only import a car you can’t bear to part with.

If you just need a commuter vehicle in Italy, it would be easier and more cost-effective to sell your current car in America and get a new car or scooter in Italy.

## Budgeting for your overseas move

We won’t sugarcoat it: moving to Italy is going to cost you thousands of dollars. Between paying your moving costs, getting a house or apartment, and paying your visa fees, this move is probably going to tap out your finances, at least for a while.

Luckily, since the visa process takes several months, you’ve got plenty of time to save up. Below, we’ll break down a few costs you should expect to pay so you can start budgeting now.

### How much does it cost to relocate to Italy?

Expect to spend somewhere between $6,000 and $13,000 (or more in some cases) to ship your household goods from the US to Italy. As with any type of move, the amount of stuff you have, the exact locations you’re moving from and to, and your shipping method can all affect your price, which is why this range is so wide.

At the end of the day, you’ll only know for sure how much your move to Italy will cost after you get an estimate from an international moving company. Your moving costs will be one of your biggest expenses, so you should start getting quotes as soon as you decide to move. Otherwise, you’ll only have a vague idea of how much money to save.

If these high costs make your dreams of moving to Italy seem unattainable, perhaps we can help. We’ve put together a guide to [paying for your move](https://www.move.org/how-to-finance-a-move/), even when it seems like you can’t.

#### Visa and immigration fees

Unfortunately, consular fees vary by which Italian consulate you get your visa through, and they change quarterly. [\[3\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources) To get up-to-date information on visa and immigration fees, check the website of whichever [Italian consulate](https://ambwashingtondc.esteri.it/ambasciata_washington/en/informazioni_e_servizi/la_rete_consolare) has jurisdiction in your state.

## Request your codice fiscale

Aside from your travel visa, your _codice fiscale_ is the most important document for your stay in Italy, and you’ll actually need your codice fiscale to apply for your visa. This document includes your Italian taxpayer identification number, which you’ll need even if you aren’t a taxpaying citizen in Italy yet.

“Codice fiscale” roughly translates to “fiscal code,” and you can think of this document as the Italian equivalent of a social security card. Unlike your social security card, though, you’ll use your codice fiscale all the time. Here are a few of the things you’ll do in Italy that require a codice fiscale:

- Opening a bank account
- Opening a postal account
- Signing a lease
- Starting utility services
- Signing contracts [\[4\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

Luckily, getting your codice fiscale is actually pretty simple compared to getting a visa, and—best of all—it’s free. You’ll just need to fill out the application form and send it in PDF form to your local Italian consulate along with PDF versions of your birth certificate, your ID, and a document proving you currently live within your consular district. [\[5\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

Be aware that the [Italian consulate](https://ambwashingtondc.esteri.it/ambasciata_washington/en/informazioni_e_servizi/la_rete_consolare) in your area might have other requirements for applying for a codice fiscale, so you should check its website before assembling your documents.

## Renew your documents

Before your move, you should make sure your passport, driver’s license, medical records, and insurance documents are all up to date. Renewing these documents is much harder for an American living abroad, so you’ll want to ensure they’ll remain valid for at least a few years after you move.

The renewal process for these documents can take a few months, so it’s good to take care of this step sooner than later.

## Apply for the visa stamp you need

Without a visa, you can only stay in Italy for 90 days at a time with a valid passport. After those 90 days, you’ll have to leave the country for 90 days before returning. Making this setup work will require insane amounts of travel on your part, and it’ll make jet lag a way of life. To live in Italy for longer than three months, you’ll need to apply for a visa.

There are many types of visas, however, and they’re meant for different people. Someone studying abroad in Italy will need a different visa from someone who intends to work there or retire there. To find out which visa is right for you, take [this survey](https://vistoperitalia.esteri.it/) from the Directorate General for Italians Abroad and Migration Policies.

#### Requirements for different types of visas

The application process is a little different for [every type of visa](https://consnewyork.esteri.it/consolato_newyork/en/i_servizi/per_chi_si_reca_in_italia/visas-to-enter.html), and each one will require different documentation. To get started on the lengthy application process, check out these guides from the Italian consulate in New York:

- [Student visas](https://consnewyork.esteri.it/consolato_newyork/en/i_servizi/per_chi_si_reca_in_italia/studenti.html)
- [Work visas](https://consnewyork.esteri.it/consolato_newyork/en/i_servizi/per_chi_si_reca_in_italia/lavorosubordinato.html)
- [Elective residency visas](https://consnewyork.esteri.it/consolato_newyork/en/i_servizi/per_chi_si_reca_in_italia/residenza.html)
- [Visas for family of US military members](https://consnewyork.esteri.it/consolato_newyork/en/i_servizi/per_chi_si_reca_in_italia/militari.html)

Keep in mind that the New York consulate might not be the one you’ll apply through, and the consulate that serves your area might have unique requirements for visa applications. To get the most accurate info for your situation, check the website of [your local Italian](https://ambwashingtondc.esteri.it/ambasciata_washington/en/informazioni_e_servizi/la_rete_consolare) [consulate](https://ambwashingtondc.esteri.it/ambasciata_washington/en/informazioni_e_servizi/la_rete_consolare).

### Packing for your flight

Flying internationally for a vacation may require careful packing, but it’s nothing compared to the packing requirements for living abroad. You’ll need to pack much more deliberately and generously for this trip than any other trip you’ve probably taken. So much for traveling light.

It will take your movers several weeks to deliver your stuff to your new home in Italy, so you should fly with everything you’ll need in the meantime. Pack plenty of clothes, all your medications, and every document you’ll need to start your new life in Italy.

Unfortunately, this probably means you’ll need to check more luggage than usual. This will be costly, but it beats living in a foreign country without the things you require.

You should also go to your bank to get plenty of euros before your flight. And if you’ve already opened a [bank account in Italy](https://www.bancaditalia.it/) (which we recommend), make sure you have your Italian debit or credit cards in your wallet.

## Apply for Italian citizenship

There are three ways to become an Italian citizen: by descent, by marriage, and by residency. [\[7\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

### How to become an Italian citizen by descent

In order to become an Italian citizen by descent, you need to be closely descended from an Italian citizen. If either of your parents, either of your grandfathers, or any of your great-grandfathers were citizens of Italy, you can apply for dual citizenship with Italy.

This will require you to substantiate official documentation proving your heritage, but it’s still the easiest way to become an Italian citizen if it applies to you.

### How to become an Italian citizen by marriage

To become an Italian citizen through marriage, you’ll first need to marry an Italian citizen. Afterward, you’ll have to wait a few years. If you live in Italy, you can apply for citizenship after two years of marriage. If you don’t live in Italy, you’ll have to wait three years. [\[8\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

Two important notes on this method:

1. Civil unions count as marriages for the purposes of gaining citizenship. [\[9\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)
2. Same-sex marriages are recognized as civil unions in Italy, so they also count. [\[10\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

### How to become an Italian citizen by residency

The third path to citizenship takes the longest, but it’s the only one available to you if you aren’t descended from or married to an Italian. Here’s how it works:

- You’ll need to hold your permesso di soggiorno for five years. This will require frequent renewals.
- After five years, you can apply for permanent resident status.
- After another five years as a permanent resident, you can then apply for Italian citizenship by residency. [\[11\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

There are a few more hoops to jump through—like passing an Italian language test—before you’ll obtain citizenship this way, but that’s the gist of it.

## FAQ about moving to Italy

### Can I live in Italy without a job?

It’s technically possible to move to Italy without a job, and some visas require that you don’t work while you’re in Italy. However, if you aren’t independently wealthy, you’ll want to get a work visa and find a way to earn money in Italy before you move there.

### What is the primary currency in Italy?

Italy is part of the European Union, so its official currency is the euro. This has been the case since 1999 when the euro replaced the Italian lira. [\[12\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources)

### Does Italy have universal health care?

Yes, Italian citizens and legal foreign residents of Italy both enjoy universal health coverage for things like primary care, inpatient care, and maternity care. [\[13\]](https://www.move.org/how-to-move-to-italy/#Sources) Visitors to Italy have to pay for their health care, though, so until you gain residency in Italy, you’ll need to procure [private health insurance](https://www.internationalinsurance.com/health/europe/italy.php).

## Your Italy Travel Planner and Expat Guide

UNCOVERING AUTHENTIC ITALY

## for travelers and expats who are ready to go beyond ‘la dolce vita’

[I'M READY TO LEARN MORE](https://collineallemontagne.com/an-american-living-in-italy/)

There’s no denying it, Italy is what dreams are made of. It’s a land of breathtaking views, dreamy Mediterranean beach coves, delicious plates of pasta, strong coffee, passionate people and flying hand gestures.

But… everyone knows that side of Italy.

You want more. Whether you’re working to make Italy home or planning your dream Italian vacation, you want to discover the _**real**_ Italy. The authentic soul of this land we all fall in love with.

You want to skip the kitsch tourist restaurant and head straight for the _trattoria_ loved by the Italian man of your dreams. You want to explore ancient Italian _borghi_, vineyards, and mountains, not just the Instagram hotspots. You want to find the lesser-known artworks hidden in plain sight.

That’s where I come in…

## Meet Your Italy Travel Planner & Expat Guide

[LEARN MORE](https://collineallemontagne.com/an-american-living-in-italy/)

## Italy Travel Planner

_More Than Just Another Grand Tour_

You’re planning the Italian vacation of a lifetime—but not the one packed with bus tours, long lines, and mediocre guidebook stops. You want the good stuff: hilltop villages, crisp alpine air, secret wine sips, and trails that don’t show up on TripAdvisor.

I’ve got you.

Whether you need a 1:1 consult to untangle your ideas, curated picks for hikes, wineries, and restuarants, or a custom-built itinerary—I’ll help you plan a trip that feels like the authentic Italy you really came for.

[YOUR ITALY EXPERIENCE AWAITS](https://collineallemontagne.com/dream-vacation-in-italy/)

### SUBITO

### Right away! Immediately!

You, “Un caffé, per favore.”

The cute Italian barista, “Subito!”

### BOH

### Means, ‘I don’t know’. Almost always accompanied by a shrug and downturned lips.

Your Italian fidanzato, “What do you want for dinner tonight?”

You, “boh.”

## Italy Expat Guide

_Make Italy Home_

You’re ready to turn your dream into a reality and Make Italy Home, or you’ve already made the move but the bureaucracy isn’t easy… Where do you even begin?

From assistance with choosing the right visa to understanding your _Permesso di Soggiorno_, you'll find so much help in my blog.

Have a look around, and if there's something missing, get in touch.

[I'M READY TO MAKE ITALY HOME](https://collineallemontagne.com/life-in-italy-blog/)

![Captured at Centro Storico on {iptoday0} Jan, 2022 by Rhianna May Photography](https://cdn.weeknightwebsite.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/1749/bb-plugin/cache/37119E5D-3D34-4D5D-9D37-5284A0BD6684-square-5eed60297d64678eca2bc1eb42ce9532-38hiboms9rej.jpeg)

## Hey, I’m Evelyn!

I love being outdoors, learning, and sharing. And I tend to get overexcited about beautiful old buildings and a great aperitivo, but **what I really love is Italy**.

13 years have gone by since I first began to call Italy home and I’ve learnt to love it in a new and complicated way. One that goes way beyond the overhyped “dolce vita”.

I’ve felt the pure elation at reaching the top of one of Italy's 3000 peaks (4k still in the works), the impossible frustration of renewing yet another Permesso, and the beautiful calm of sitting in a busy piazza with a spritz, just watching the world go by.

But one of my greatest joys since moving here? The chance to share my love and understanding of the _**real**_ Italy with you.

[WANT TO GET TO KNOW ME?](https://collineallemontagne.com/an-american-living-in-italy/)

“I wanted to let you know how amazing your service is! I took a massive leap into the unknown world of visa uncertainty when I followed my heart and came to Italy in December 2020. I’d done some zoom calls with a lawyer in Rome to get some advice, but it’s thanks to your work that I feel confident to find my path forward and continue my life in Italy. Thank you!!”

\- Ann-Maree

Italy is a country with a rich, vibrant culture and, as an American moving to Italy, you’ll want to have an understanding of their culture before your relocation. This includes etiquette and their appreciation for dining and socialization.

If you're moving to an urban area, many Italians will speak English; in rural areas, it’s not as common. In general, the cost of living will be less in Italy although the gap will be more significant in rural areas and less in cities.

Italy has an outstanding health care system, but you’ll want to be clear about whether private insurance is a good idea while you’re transitioning to your new country. ## FAQs

Frequently Asked Questions about Moving

What items are prohibited when moving to Italy?

Weapons, certain electronics, and perishable foods are restricted — see the [FIDI Customs Guide](https://www.fidi.org/customs-guides).

Do I pay import duties when moving to Italy?

Used household goods are typically duty-free under re-entry rules.

How long does customs clearance take in Italy?

Clearance usually takes 1–2 weeks depending on documentation accuracy.

Can I move with pets to Italy?

Yes, with microchip, rabies vaccination, and veterinary certificate ( [EU Commission](https://food.ec.europa.eu/animals/movement-pets_en)).

# Relocation Services to Italy

A&P provides professional assistance to employees, families and individuals who need to relocate to Italy for work, live or retire in Italy.

[Contact us for assistance](https://arlettipartners.com/services/relocation-services-move-to-italy/#contact)

[Book a call​](https://arlettipartners.com/online-consultation/move-to-italy-ap-relocation-services/)

### Which country the service is available for:

Italy

## What our services entail

**Finding a new home** can be stressful and time consuming, especially if you are considering from your own country. Real-estate market isreally fast-paced and **in-person meetings are preferred over online ones**. Thanks to ourunderstanding of the market, **we****can support** in arrangingprofitablevisitsafter yourarrival.

- **Tour and accomodation**: get to know the city while waiting for your new home at a temporary accomodation;
- **Home research**: weselectunitsbased on yourrequirements and accompanyyouduring house visits;
- **Contract Negotiations**: after youhaveselectedyour future house, we’ll support you in understandingthe leasing conditions and guide youthrough the processuntil the keys delivery;
- **Settle in services**: wewill support youupon the keys delivery to check and record the house conditions and we will provide full assistance to set up basic utilities.

## Move wherever you want!

We can provide full support all around Italy through our network of local consultants. Every city has its peculirarities, thanks to our experience we will guide you through the local real estate market and discuss the best strategy for an effective house hunting. Check our guides to move in [**Bologna**](https://arlettipartners.com/move-to-bologna/), [**Parma**](https://arlettipartners.com/moving-to-parma-why-parma-may-be-the-right-city-for-you/)& [**Modena**](https://arlettipartners.com/life-in-modena-things-you-should-know-moving-to-emilia-romagna/)!

## What should I consider before moving to Italy?

**Before** planning your move to Italy, please **keep in mind** that citizens need to **fulfill** **immigration**, **social security and taxation requirements**​. **A&P** can help you identify your **specific fullfillments**:

- **Immigration requirements** for non-EU citizens;
- **Driving in Italy** and car registration;
- Access to **National Healthcare System**;
- **Townhall registration** and its tax implications;
- Support with the **Italian ID Card**;
- Support with the **school search**.

## If you are an Italian citizen moving from abroad you will need:

- **Registration** with the **registry office** and **removal** from the **AIRE** (Registry of Italians Resident Abroad);
- Once residency has been established, **obtaining a primary care physician**;
- **Immigration support** for spouses and **family members** from **outside the EU**;
- **Car registration** as a repatriated citizen.

Residents benefit from access to medical services, organized municipal systems, and public infrastructure supporting everyday life.

Transporting personal belongings internationally requires compliance with customs regulations. Shipment inventories, documentation, and declarations must be prepared to ensure household goods can be cleared smoothly when arriving in Italy.
